Chapter 7: Speaking Up — Advocacy, Boundaries, and the Power of Saying No.
You know, there comes a point in life when staying silent just feels heavier than actually speaking up. For her, that moment didn’t happen all at once. It crept up, shaped by years of seeing people—especially women—get dismissed, belittled, or simply ignored. The urge to advocate, to use her own voice for something bigger, kept growing.
She wasn’t looking to be a hero. It was just about not letting fear or shame call the shots anymore. So, she started small. Maybe it was calling out a rude comment, standing up for a friend, or refusing to laugh at a joke that crossed the line. Every time she spoke up, it felt risky—but it also felt absolutely necessary.
What surprised her? The more she spoke out, the more she realized just how many others were waiting for someone—anyone—to go first. There’s something powerful about one honest voice. Most people don’t realize the ripple effect it can have.
Boundaries became her lifeline. In a world that always seemed to want more, learning to say no felt like an act of self-preservation. She started to decline invitations, walk away from projects, and let go of relationships that drained her. Sure, the guilt and second-guessing showed up every time. But so did a growing sense of freedom.
It turns out, setting boundaries isn’t selfish. It’s about protecting your energy so you can stay true to your values. Imagine that—guarding your own wellbeing, even if it means disappointing someone else.
One moment really stands out. She was backstage when a colleague made a joke at her expense. That old urge to just laugh it off was strong. But this time, something in her shifted. She spoke up—calmly, firmly—and the whole room went quiet. Later, another woman pulled her aside and thanked her. That’s when she realized: courage is contagious. Every time someone stands up, it gets a little bit easier for the next person.
Advocacy, for her, took all kinds of forms. Sometimes it was big—talking publicly about body image, sexual assault, or the challenges women face in comedy. Other times, it was quieter—just listening to a friend, offering support, or sharing her own story. That kind of work can be exhausting, but it’s also deeply rewarding. She saw how honesty could break down walls, and how being vulnerable could actually create real connection.
Over time, she learned that advocacy isn’t about being perfect or knowing all the answers. It’s about showing up, telling the truth, and making space for others to do the same. And the power of saying no—of drawing a line and holding it—became one of her greatest strengths.
Most people never see how much strength it takes to disappoint someone else just to stay true to yourself. But for her, that was the only way to keep moving forward.
